newsitem.title: USA: EPA expected to push tougher air quality standards.
newsitem.headline: EPA expected to push tougher air quality standards.

text.p: In a move pitting industries against health advocates, federal regulators next month are expected to propose stricter limits on air pollution from smog-forming gases and tiny particles that may lodge in lungs.

Industry and some fossil fuel groups charge that rules the Environmental Protection Agency plans to push would cost them billions of dollars, jeopardise jobs and irritate consumers for what they say would be small or unproven health benefits.
But health and environmental groups say with strong new rules the EPA would prolong tens of thousands of lives each year and improve the health of millions.

"It's one of the biggest issues we're facing," said Richard Siebert, vice president for resources, environment and regulation of the National Association of Manufacturers, which is spearheading lobbying against tighter controls.

"The effects ... would be loss of federal monies, loss of job expansion, and significant lifestyle changes -- not only reduced driving, but outdoor barbeques, use of power machinery, boating," Siebert said.

The American Lung Association and other advocacy groups in a letter to President Clinton called the standards "the most important public health decision EPA will make this year." They urged him to "support standards that protect all Americans, especially the most vulnerable -- the young, the elderly and people with lung diseases like asthma."

Deborah Shprentz of the Natural Resources Defence Council said more than 60,000 Americans die prematurely each year because of air particle pollution. "Except for smoking there's really no other opportunity to effect as much improvement in environmental health as by controlling this particulate pollution," she said.

The EPA likely will propose tougher rules but it is less certain what the agency will finally adopt next June after months of hammering by lobbyists on both sides. Its current standard for ozone -- or smog-forming gases -- allows a maximum concentration of 0.12 parts per million measured over a one-hour period. It is considering lowering the maximum allowable concentration to 0.07-0.09 parts per million.

The agency currently regulates air particles that are 10 microns and smaller in diameter -- small enough to enter lungs -- to maximum concentrations of 150 micrograms per cubic meter averaged over 24 hours. But it is considering a separate standard for finer particles of 2.5 microns and smaller, which health experts say are more dangerous because they delve deep into lung tissue.

Clean air advocates want a strict standard for fine particles and they want the EPA to tighten the standard aimed at larger particles, which are a serious problem in many Western states because of dust and use of wood stoves.

Industry groups say a strict rule for the smallest particles would affect nearly all combustion sources, including cars, and would throw many Eastern cities out of compliance with air quality standards.
Because the EPA has not monitored for the fine particle exposure before, industry groups also argue it does not have data or science on its side in requiring strict controls.

"I characterise this as the classic situation of ready, fire, aim," said Richard Klimisch, the American Automobile Manufacturers Association's vice president of engineering. He said the EPA should monitor now and set new rules later.

Congress, in non-binding language in a budget bill Clinton signed last month, said the agency did not have enough data and should keep the current particulate standard. But clean air advocates say research shows that air particles within current legal levels are shortening lives.

"The medical research clearly indicates that the longer we wait to set and meet the tighter health standard for air pollution, the more premature deaths and hospitalizations caused by air pollution will occur," advocacy groups said in a letter to EPA Administrator Carol Browner.
